analysis.one_liner: Requires lenders to hold a mediation with a homeowner and a housing counselor, at the lender's expense, before foreclosing on federally backed home loans.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: introduced December 18, 2009, it sat in the Senate Banking Committee until the Congress ended, with only two of 58 Senate Democrats supporting it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required lenders on most federally backed home mortgages — FHA, VA, rural housing, and anything Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac could buy — to hold a one-time mediation with the homeowner and a certified housing counselor before starting a foreclosure or sheriff sale. The lender, not the homeowner, would pay for it. The aim was to give families facing foreclosure a real chance to work out an alternative before losing their home, at a time when foreclosures were surging nationwide, especially in sponsor Bill Nelson's home state of Florida.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners facing foreclosure on a federally backed mortgage — FHA, VA, rural housing, or any loan eligible for Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac purchase — would get a free, mandatory sit-down with their lender and a certified housing counselor before a foreclosure could be filed or a home sold at sheriff sale. Many families in default do not know their options, and servicers routinely miss paperwork or offer alternatives only under pressure; a required meeting would force the lender to show up and consider a workout, including in cases where the party suing (such as a MERS nominee) does not actually hold the loan.

how_it_helps.text: Before starting a foreclosure or a sheriff sale, the lender would have to hold a one-time mediation with the homeowner and a certified housing counseling agency — and pay for it out of the lender's own pocket.

The requirement covered most home mortgages a typical family could have: loans federally insured, guaranteed, or made through FHA, VA, and rural housing programs, or eligible for purchase by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac, and it explicitly reached the mortgagee of record, including MERS, so homeowners would not be stalled by disputes over who actually holds their loan.
Because a housing counseling agency had to take part, homeowners would get professional advice at the table rather than facing the lender's paperwork alone.

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders and loan servicers would pay for the mediation and bear the cost of delaying foreclosures, since the bill barred starting a foreclosure or sheriff sale until the meeting took place. Lenders would also lose some of the speed and leverage of the foreclosure pipeline during a period of record defaults.

drawbacks.text: Mediation addresses process, not affordability: a homeowner whose income cannot support any modification may still lose the home after the one-time meeting, and the bill offered no new funds for loan write-downs or payment relief.

Mandating a meeting before every foreclosure on the vast universe of federally backed loans (anything eligible for purchase by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac) could slow the housing market's recovery by delaying foreclosures lenders argue should proceed quickly, and the bill put the cost on lenders, who might pass servicing expenses along to other borrowers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a final, independent sit-down between a family and their lender, with a certified counselor present, before a foreclosure goes forward — is real and targeted: it reaches precisely the loans where federal backing gives the government the clearest authority to impose conditions. The costs are modest and fall on the industry: one mediation per loan, paid for by the lender, with the risk of some foreclosure delays and added servicing workload. A reasonable objection is that mediation alone may not save many homes when the underlying problem is the homeowner cannot afford the payment at all, and that a one-size federal mandate could slow even foreclosures that no one disputes. On balance the design is narrow and inexpensive relative to the scale of the crisis it addressed; its biggest flaw is that it never received any committee consideration.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-December 2009, sent straight to the Senate Banking Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Nelson of Florida introduced the bill on December 18, 2009, during the height of the national foreclosure wave.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — and the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 with the bill still in committee.
Only two of the Senate's 58 Democrats signed on as cosponsors, so the bill had minimal support to push it out of committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and servicers came out ahead: they faced no mediation requirement or added foreclosure costs, and no delay in proceeding with foreclosures. Families facing foreclosure gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Bill Nelson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Banking Committee, where it received no further action.

against.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; the sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican senator took any recorded action on the bill either way.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to fund and attend a mediation before every foreclosure on a federally backed loan, adding cost and delay to the foreclosure process and forcing loan holders (including MERS nominees) to face homeowners in person. Lenders instead proceeded with foreclosures without any such meeting.

The bill would have routed every pre-foreclosure mediation through HUD-certified housing counseling agencies or Neighborhood Reinvestment programs, making them a required participant in the process and a channel for public foreclosure relief. Because the bill died, this role was never locked in.
